A Unified Arena for LLM Agents
across Diverse Eurogames

Fengrui Zhang1,2, Xiang Li3, Ruomeng Ding4, Jiayi Yuan, Yuchen Huang5 Zhaoyang Han6, Xiaoliang Wang2, Daoyuan Chen1, Yaliang Li1 1Alibaba Group 2Nanjing University
3National University of Singapore
4Department of Computer Science, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
5The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
6Peking University
Abstract

Interactive environments offer a practical way to evaluate large language model (LLM) agents, and competitive games extend this evaluation to decisions shaped by competing goals and other agents’ choices. Yet existing evaluations confined to individual games or execution frameworks leave unclear which competitive advantages persist across settings. We introduce DECE (Diverse Eurogame Competitive Environments), a unified arena spanning ten Eurogames with shared interfaces and evaluation protocols. These games combine lasting strategic commitments, competition over shared resources, and multiple routes to victory. Our primary study evaluates 12 model–harness configurations, spanning nine models and four execution harnesses, in 480 three-player matches across ten games. The main and supplementary studies comprise 1,032 completed matches in total. These comparisons reveal broad cross-game ranking agreement alongside game-specific strengths. Matched studies show that the same model can perform differently across execution harnesses, adding another source of variation to these profiles. These performance advantages do not consistently translate into better token or cost efficiency, making resource use an additional consideration when comparing configurations. Together, the findings support evaluating complete agent configurations by both their competitive performance across games and the resources needed to achieve it.

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly act through tools in external environments (Yao et al., 2023). Interactive benchmarks evaluate their decisions over extended trajectories (Liu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024). In competition, opponents pursue their own objectives and change an agent’s available opportunities. An action’s value depends on both its future consequences and opponents’ choices. We ask:

How can competitive environments support reliable evaluation of

complete agent systems across diverse strategic demands?

Strategy board games make this question tractable. They combine explicit rules, programmatically executable states and actions, and independently verifiable outcomes (Gaina et al., 2020; Balla et al., 2024). Their interactions can be represented as partially observable stochastic games (POSGs) (Hansen et al., 2004). Agents act on their observation histories; their actions determine state transitions and outcomes. We focus on Eurogames (German-style strategy board games), which combine persistent investments, competition over shared opportunities, and multiple routes to victory. In Splendor, development cards reduce later purchase costs; Azul placements constrain future spatial scoring (Space Cowboys, n.d.; Next Move Games, n.d.). These commitments shape both a player’s future options and opponents’ opportunities.

Existing multi-game benchmarks and harness studies provide foundations for competitive evaluation (Costarelli et al., 2024; Hua et al., 2026). Turning these games into a common benchmark presents three challenges. Agents need consistent observation–action interfaces across diverse rules and information structures, while retaining their tools and context management. Analysis must distinguish recurring competitive strength from game-specific advantages and account for execution settings and resource use. Reliable comparisons require consistent rule enforcement, a common participant roster, seat-balanced protocols, and verifiable outcomes. Matched scenarios and uncertainty estimates support comparisons of execution settings.

We introduce DECE (Diverse Eurogame Competitive Environments), a unified evaluation framework spanning ten executable Eurogames.11 1 The name also echoes dé cè, a Chinese shorthand for Euro-style strategy board games. The games vary in their demands for economic development, spatial commitment, and coordination across scoring routes while retaining a shared competitive structure. As illustrated in Figure 1, a common interface exposes seat-specific observations and legal actions to pluggable execution harnesses. Each participant is a complete model–harness configuration, including its tools and context management. A common roster and seat-balanced protocols support cross-game comparisons. Separate matched studies compare the same model across harnesses, fixing setup seeds, focal seats, and opponent configurations within each scenario. Game engines enforce rules and scoring; execution records support auditing and outcome checks. We quantify uncertainty by resampling whole matches or matched scenarios. We report token use and API-equivalent cost under a fixed pricing schedule alongside competitive outcomes.

Our evaluation comprises 1,032 completed matches across the main and supplementary studies. The primary study evaluates 12 model–harness configurations, spanning nine models and four harnesses, in 480 three-player matches across ten games. Rankings formed on nine games agree with the held-out game at mean Kendall τb=0.664\tau_{b}=0.664 and 83.9% pair-order accuracy. Game-level profiles reveal distinct strengths and local reversals that the aggregate ranking obscures. Separate matched studies show that the same model’s performance can differ across execution harnesses. Performance–resource trade-offs vary across games, and token-based and cost-based comparisons favor different configurations. These findings support evaluating complete agent systems across multiple competitive environments, with game-level profiles and resource use reported alongside aggregate rankings.

Section 2 reviews related benchmarks. Section 3 presents DECE’s environments and evaluation protocol. Section 4 examines cross-game performance profiles (RQ1), matched harness comparisons (RQ2), and game-specific performance–resource trade-offs (RQ3). Section 5 discusses implications for competitive agent evaluation.

2 Related Work

Games provide a natural setting for evaluating LLM agents because they combine explicit rules, sequential interaction, and verifiable outcomes. Recent benchmarks span both digital and tabletop environments: Orak, BALROG, and LMGame-Bench evaluate agents across video games (Park et al., 2026; Paglieri et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026a) , while GameBench and MindGames study competitive and social reasoning in board, card, and strategy games (Costarelli et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026). FinBoardBench studies financial decisions and PTCG-Bench examines card play, harness ablations, self-evolution, and cost (Hu et al., 2026b; Hua et al., 2026). Complementary work such as TAG and From Code to Play provides executable tabletop environments or evaluates components used by search-based players (Gaina et al., 2020; Eberhardinger et al., 2024), while LudoBench studies reasoning from fixed game states (Peper et al., 2026).

Position of DECE.

DECE compares complete agent configurations across ten Eurogames with persistent investments, spatial commitments, and multiple scoring routes. A common roster measures cross-game agreement and local strengths; matched studies assess harness contrasts, and game-specific frontiers relate performance to dollars and tokens. Table 1 compares the benchmark scope.

3 DECE: Benchmark Design and Evaluation Protocol

3.1 Game suite and strategic diversity

DECE selects ten score-based Eurogames that share persistent strategic commitments and competition over limited opportunities, while differing in how current decisions shape future options. Table 2 groups them by three dominant, overlapping demands: building future capacity, making persistent spatial commitments, and coordinating multiple action, resource, and scoring systems. These differences allow the suite to test whether competitive advantages recur across related strategic settings or remain specific to individual games. The games also vary in interaction and information structure: players compete entirely through legal game actions, without dialogue or negotiation, and decisions may involve public or private information as well as sequential or simultaneous choices.

Figure 2 characterizes this diversity along six rule-based dimensions: engine construction, spatial planning, action sequencing, opponent coupling, hidden information, and scoring coordination. Values 0/1/2 denote absent, limited, or prominent mechanisms. These annotations organize descriptive cross-game comparisons (Appendix B). The suite also spans substantially different interaction lengths, with median whole-match decision counts ranging from 54 in 7 Wonders to 473 in Ark Nova. These counts summarize interaction length at each interface’s action granularity (Appendix C).

3.2 Unified game interface and participant abstraction

All games share an interface for setup, seat-specific observations, legal actions, state transitions, and terminal rankings. The engine enforces rules and scoring. Simultaneous choices use a frozen state and advance only after all required seats submit actions. Public information, private state, and unrevealed randomness remain separate. MCP and native adapters expose this interface; persisted states and execution records support auditing, replay, and resume (Appendix A.3).

Each participant specifies a model snapshot, execution harness, prompts, tools, memory scope, inference settings, and resource budget. The shared interface permits different internal histories and orchestration strategies. The primary panel contains 12 configurations spanning nine model identities and four harnesses (Appendix A.2). Comparisons evaluate these complete configurations.

3.3 Competitive outcomes and resource accounting

We convert terminal placements into pairwise wins, assigning half credit for ties, and fit regularized Bradley–Terry ratings on an Elo scale (Bradley and Terry, 1952):

pi​j=11+10(Ej−Ei)/400,Ei=1500+400ln⁡10​θi,∑iθi=0.p_{ij}=\frac{1}{1+10^{(E_{j}-E_{i})/400}},\qquad E_{i}=1500+\frac{400}{\ln 10}\theta_{i},\quad\sum_{i}\theta_{i}=0. (1)

Ratings express relative strength and are centered within each comparison population. Appendix E specifies fitting and uncertainty.

Pairwise placement score (PWS) is the fraction of opponents outranked, with half credit for ties. Mean PWS weights the ten games equally. Additional player counts are analyzed separately, and uncertainty uses whole-match resampling (Appendix D.2).

We pair three-player outcomes with input-plus-output tokens and API-equivalent cost under a fixed pricing schedule. Per-game Elo–cost and Elo–token frontiers retain configurations for which no alternative achieves at least as high performance with no greater resource use (Appendix E).

4 Experimental Evaluation

4.1 Cohorts and uncertainty

The main comparison contains 480 three-player matches across ten games: 144 from the original Splendor, 7 Wonders, and Brass cohort, plus 336 from the seven-game expansion. Each game contributes 48 matches and 12 appearances per participant, balanced across seats. Another 252 two- or four-player matches support player-count analysis, giving 732 native-system matches in total. All outcomes reconcile with schedules and final records (Appendix D.7). Table 3 reports the three-player cohort; PWS means weight games equally. Its column groups follow Figure 2. Pointwise 95% intervals use 5,000 whole-match bootstrap draws per game, recomputing PWS and refitting Elo while retaining the ten games (Appendix D.3).

We completed 180 matches for three non-LLM algorithms—Random, Heuristic, and ISMCTS—in separate 60-match cohorts. Their PWS scores gauge their approximate competitive standing relative to the 12 LLM participants (Table 3). Each cohort contains six three-player matches per game against two LLM opponents. The three cohorts use identical games, rules, setup seeds, opponent configurations, and seat assignments; only the baseline algorithm changes (Appendix D.8).

Two independent studies cross OpenCode and Qwen Code in Splendor and 7 Wonders. The 72-match bridge pairs DSV4-Flash with Qwen3.8-Flash across nine scenarios per game; the 48-match within-Qwen-family study pairs Qwen3.8-Flash with Qwen3.8-Max across six. Within each study, those models under OpenCode serve as anchors. Each scenario fixes the setup seed and focal seat across four matches, with balanced seats. Pointwise intervals resample whole scenarios. Each study retains its own anchors and analysis, separate from the native ratings (Appendices G and G.3).

4.2 RQ1: Cross-game performance profiles

Aggregate rankings generalize across games.

Nine-game mean PWS rankings agree with the held-out game at mean Kendall τb=0.664\tau_{b}=0.664 and 83.9% pair-order accuracy; per-game τb\tau_{b} ranges from 0.489 to 0.862. These results support recurring cross-game rankings alongside local variation; Appendix D.3 gives ranking uncertainty and split-half diagnostics.

Broad strength and concentrated advantages.

GPT-5.6-Sol/OpenCode and GPT-5.6-Sol/Codex lead equal-game PWS at 75.6% and 75.4%; both remain above 50% in every game and within the top five by three-player Elo. Their 0.2 pp difference has a whole-match interval of [−-8.6, 9.3]. Qwen3.8-Max/Qwen Code has lower mean PWS (70.2%) but leads or ties five game columns. DSV4-Pro/DSH has no column lead, yet stays between 58.3% and 66.7% across games. These profiles distinguish broad competitiveness from local peaks and weaknesses.

Advantages recur across selected strategic settings.

Qwen3.8-Max/Qwen Code ranks first by Elo in Azul, Harmonies, and Carcassonne, and second in Burgundy. All four combine prominent spatial constraints with public current holdings under the rubric in Figure 2; their equal-game PWS is 84.9%. GPT-5.6-Terra/Codex shows a different concentration: it ranks third, second, and fourth in Century, Brass, and Ark Nova (75.0% mean PWS), but eleventh, tenth, and seventh in Azul, Harmonies, and Carcassonne (36.8%). Its ten-game mean of 50.2% conceals this separation. Together with the Qwen3.8-Max profile, this illustrates how similar aggregate summaries can arise from markedly different game-level performance patterns.

A single mechanism does not summarize the profile.

Brass and Ark Nova also have prominent spatial constraints, but Qwen3.8-Max/Qwen Code ranks sixth and eighth there. Conversely, GPT-5.6-Terra/Codex’s strong results in several economic systems do not extend to all engine-building games: it ranks tenth in Splendor and sixth in Wingspan. Averaging GPT-5.6-Terra over all spatial games gives 51.0% PWS, versus 49.0% elsewhere, masking substantial differences within that group. These counterexamples motivate examining combinations of commitments, information, and action dependencies rather than assigning a model one domain label.

Configuration advantages across game groups.

The preceding examples suggest that some configuration differences may recur across games sharing particular rule properties. We therefore ask whether same-model harness differences are concentrated within a rule-defined subset of games rather than cancelling when averaged across the full suite. For each model, δg\delta_{g} is its PWS under harness A minus its PWS under OpenCode in game gg, measured in percentage points. Group GG comprises Azul, Harmonies, Carcassonne, and Burgundy; HH contains the other six games. All four games have spatial planning = 2 and hidden information = 0 under the rule annotations in Figure 2. This criterion differs from the dominant strategic emphases used in Tables 2 and 3, where Burgundy belongs to Coordination.

Let Δ¯G\overline{\Delta}_{G} and Δ¯H\overline{\Delta}_{H} denote the equal-game means of δg\delta_{g} in each group. Their difference, Γ=Δ¯G−Δ¯H\Gamma=\overline{\Delta}_{G}-\overline{\Delta}_{H}, measures how the average configuration advantage differs between groups. A positive Γ\Gamma indicates that harness A has a larger average advantage over OpenCode in the public-spatial group than in the remaining games. These contrasts describe configuration performance across the rule-defined game groups under the native opponent samples. Appendix D.4 gives the interval and game-deletion procedures.

Table 4 separates recurring advantages from cancellation across games. Qwen3.8-Max/Qwen Code exceeds OpenCode in all four public-spatial games (+10.4 to +41.7 pp). Its zero mean advantage elsewhere masks gains in Splendor (+20.8) and losses in Ark Nova (−33.3-33.3). The between-group difference is +29.7 pp [11.9, 46.9] and ranges from +23.0 to +36.1 when one game is omitted.

The other pairs have different profiles: GPT-5.6-Sol/Codex has three negative and one zero contrast in the public-spatial group, while DSV4-Pro/DSH has two positive and two negative contrasts. Game deletion preserves the sign of the Qwen3.8-Max and GPT-5.6-Sol group differences, whereas DSV4-Pro’s range crosses zero. These composition checks complement the sampling intervals conditional on the selected groups. Appendix D.4 gives further sensitivity checks; RQ2 examines separate model panels under matched scenarios.

These comparisons fix three players. Appendix F.1 reports supplementary player-count results and their opponent-composition scope.

4.3 RQ2: Performance across harnesses

The native-cohort comparisons in Section 4.2 suggest that the same registered model can exhibit different game-level profiles across harnesses, but these comparisons involve different opponent samples. We therefore conduct two matched studies in Splendor and 7 Wonders, fixing the setup seed, focal seat, and anchor configurations within each scenario.

Cross-model-family contrasts.

Against the shared anchors in the 72-match bridge, DSV4-Flash leads Qwen3.8-Flash under OpenCode (58.3% versus 33.3% pooled PWS); under Qwen Code, the point estimates reverse (58.3% versus 63.9%). Their difference in harness gains is +30.6 pp [−-5.6, 69.4]. Qwen3.8-Flash’s largest gain is in 7 Wonders (+44.4 pp; Figure 3a).

Within-Qwen-family contrasts.

In the 48-match within-Qwen-family study, Qwen3.8-Max’s Splendor PWS rises from 33.3% under OpenCode to 91.7% under Qwen Code, a +58.3 pp contrast [50.0, 75.0]. All six matched scenarios favor Qwen Code (Figure 3c), whereas Qwen3.8-Flash improves by only +8.3 pp in the same game. The corresponding difference in harness gains is +50.0 pp in Splendor but −-8.3 pp in 7 Wonders (Figure 3d), indicating that harness effects can vary across both models and games. The six positive Qwen3.8-Max/Splendor pairs yield a two-sided sign-test p=0.03125p=0.03125, or 0.1250.125 after correction for four model–game contrasts (Appendix G.3). We therefore view this as a strong local contrast that motivates replication, rather than evidence for a general model–harness interaction.

4.4 RQ3: Performance–resource trade-offs

For each game, we compare three-player Elo with mean API-equivalent cost per appearance under fixed prices (Figure 4). All 480 matches contribute; 5,000 whole-match resamples recompute both axes and frontier membership.

Efficient configurations depend on the game.

Point-estimate frontiers contain five to seven configurations. GPT-5.6-Luna/Codex and DSV4-Pro/DSH appear in all ten games, while GPT-5.6-Sol/OpenCode appears in nine. Qwen3.8-Max/Qwen Code lies on five frontiers, reaching the high-cost end in Wingspan (Elo 1837, $89.25), but is dominated in Burgundy and Ark Nova. GPT-5.6-Sol/Codex also lies on five frontiers and reaches the highest Elo in Brass (2068, $40.53 per appearance) and Ark Nova (2143, $37.20). For a given mean-cost budget, the staircase identifies the highest estimated Elo among affordable configurations. Moving along it shows where a higher budget changes the preferred configuration. Coverage across games describes how often a configuration is nondominated; its location within each game shows the cost and playing strength it offers.

Frontier membership has unequal sampling stability.

GPT-5.6-Sol/Codex remains nondominated in 90.3% of Brass resamples and 94.0% of Ark Nova resamples, compared with 44.3% in Splendor. Qwen3.8-Max/Qwen Code remains nondominated in 46.8% of Wingspan resamples, 69.8% in Harmonies, and 75.0% in Carcassonne. These frequencies indicate how often a configuration remains a candidate when the observed matches are resampled. They distinguish frequently retained options from positions that change with the sampled outcomes.

Token frontiers separate usage from pricing.

Using mean input-plus-output tokens yields one to six frontier configurations per game (Figure 10). GPT-5.6-Luna/Codex appears on three token frontiers, compared with ten cost frontiers; DSV4-Pro/DSH appears on two, compared with ten. Kimi-K2.7-Code/OpenCode shows the reverse pattern, appearing on six token frontiers and no dollar frontiers. The different candidate sets reflect both token consumption and the fixed rates applied to input, cached input, and output. Reporting both measures makes these sources of resource efficiency visible. Token usage is measured in each model’s native tokenizer (Appendix E).

5 Discussion and Conclusion

DECE finds both cross-game ranking agreement and local differences in competitive performance. The games share persistent investments, contested opportunities, and alternative scoring routes, while differing in rules and information structure. The shared roster reveals where advantages recur and where they reverse. Aggregate rankings summarize broad competitiveness, while game-level profiles identify settings in which a configuration becomes more or less effective.

Complete systems as the evaluation unit.

Matched comparisons connect these profiles to agent execution. The same model can perform differently across harnesses under matched scenarios. Competitive results characterize the complete model–harness configuration. Reporting tools, context management, and execution settings makes that system explicit. Cross-game comparisons show whether configuration gains recur or concentrate in particular strategic settings.

From profiles to configuration selection.

The resource frontiers identify candidate configurations for a game and budget. Future work can select configurations from game rules and results on training games. Evaluation should compare against the best generalist selected on those games, keeping target-game outcomes out of tuning. Applying the same budget to both methods would test whether game-specific selection improves competitive performance at a given resource cost. Token and dollar budgets would test distinct deployment constraints.

Limitations.

The native and matched studies evaluate complete configurations within their respective game and opponent panels. Component interventions, combined with action–outcome analyses, can test how planning and memory contribute to these performance differences.

DECE combines executable Eurogames, common tournament protocols, and resource measurements linked to competitive outcomes. Together, these elements support evaluation that reports where complete agent configurations perform well, how execution choices change their results, and what resources they require.

Appendix A Implementation Scope and Game Documentation

A.1 Implemented rules and information scope

All ten games contribute to the common three-player cohort. Table 5 lists the implemented rule versions and configuration details. Descriptions of investments, scoring, and interaction appear with their rule evidence in Appendix B.

Information and action representation.

The POSG framework accommodates private observations, public states, and sequential or simultaneous decisions (Hansen et al., 2004). DECE exposes a seat-specific observation and legal action identifiers. Public holdings, private information, unrevealed draws, and sealed choices are recorded as distinct properties. The interface has no inter-player dialogue channel. The game engine applies rules and determines outcomes; persisted states and execution records support replay and resume. Terminal outcomes undergo the checks in Appendix D.7.

Rules sources and attribution.

Publisher documentation supplies the game-design references (Space Cowboys, n.d.; Plan B Games, 2024; Next Move Games, n.d.; Hans im Glück, n.d.; Repos Production, n.d.; Libellud, n.d.; Stonemaier Games, n.d.; alea and Ravensburger, n.d.; Roxley, n.d.; Feuerland Spiele, 2022); recorded configurations determine the evaluated scope. Cover thumbnails in Figure 1 identify the games; artwork remains with the respective rights holders.

A.2 Participant identities and recorded settings

GPT-5.6-Sol, GPT-5.6-Terra, and GPT-5.6-Luna identify the three GPT-5.6 variants in the evaluated participant panel (OpenAI, 2026). The Qwen configurations use Qwen3.8-Max (Qwen Team, 2026) and Qwen3.7-Plus (Alibaba Cloud, 2026a). DSV4-Pro and DSV4-Flash denote the registered DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and V4 Flash 0731 snapshots of the DeepSeek-V4 family (DeepSeek-AI and others, 2026). GLM-5.2’s official model card (Z.ai, 2026) recommends the GLM-5 technical report (GLM-5 Team and others, 2026). The Kimi configuration uses Kimi-K2.7-Code (Moonshot AI, 2026). The separate harness bridge uses Qwen3.8-Flash (Alibaba Cloud, 2026b) and the DSV4-Flash 0731 snapshot. These reports, model cards, and release documents describe the corresponding models or families; the recorded configurations identify the evaluated snapshots. Each model–harness configuration remains one participant.

All 336 expansion results use the model strings and effort settings shown in Table 6. Controller retries and fallback actions are disabled. The matched studies use their own configurations (Appendix G).

A.3 Integration and execution

Appendix B Mechanism Profiles and Annotation Rubric

Figure 2 describes the selected games using six rule-based annotations. The authors assigned ordinal values from publisher rules and the corresponding observation interfaces. RQ1 uses these annotations to organize descriptive comparisons, with group definitions in Appendix D.4.

Annotation rubric.

Each axis uses the following anchors. A value of zero means that the defined mechanism is absent, not that a game requires no reasoning. Hidden information concerns current private holdings; uncertainty about future random draws is excluded. Spatial planning concerns geometry and connectivity, not the mere presence of rows in a tableau.

EC: Engine construction.

0: No persistent production or action modifier; 1: Localized recurring benefit or modifier; 2: Acquired assets repeatedly change action yields, costs, or available conversions.

SP: Spatial planning.

0: No geometric adjacency or connectivity constraint; 1: Geometry affects a subsidiary mechanism; 2: Adjacency, connectivity, or packing is central to placement or scoring.

AS: Action sequencing.

0: No material ordering dependency; 1: Resource or placement prerequisites create ordering constraints; 2: Explicit reuse, activation chains, action-strength cycles, or staged production dependencies.

OC: Opponent coupling.

0: Independent boards and supplies; only final score comparison; 1: Shared offers, resource pools, or races; 2: Trade or shared infrastructure, contested ownership, neighbor military comparisons, or opponent-shaped compulsory leftovers.

HI: Hidden information.

0: Current decision-relevant holdings public; future random draws excluded; 1: Limited or optional private holdings; 2: Private hands or goals are a recurrent central part of decisions.

SC: Scoring coordination.

0: One principal additive scoring conversion; 1: Main scoring route plus a secondary bonus or threshold; 2: Overlapping, nonlinear, comparative, or staged scoring objectives.

Reading the profiles.

The colors identify three overlapping strategic emphases: building future capacity, committing space and pieces, and coordinating several systems. Opponent coupling follows the main competitive mechanism in the evaluated configuration. Wingspan’s habitat order is represented under action sequencing. Century’s information annotation follows DECE’s public merchant-hand observation. Ark Nova receives OC=1 for its shared displays and project races.

Rule evidence.

The following notes explain every coordinate in axis order.

Splendor.

EC: Development bonuses permanently reduce later purchase costs. SP: Market rows and card tableaux impose no geometric scoring constraint. AS: Gem collection and discount prerequisites order purchases. OC: Shared cards, gems, and nobles create races. HI: Reserved developments can remain private. SC: Prestige purchases are supplemented by noble thresholds. (Space Cowboys, n.d.).

Century: Spice Road.

EC: Acquired merchants expand reusable resource-conversion options. SP: Card market order is a price rule, not geometric planning. AS: Played merchants require a rest action before reuse. OC: Merchant and point-card markets are shared. HI: DECE exposes merchant hands; unknown future draws do not count here. SC: Point cards dominate, with coins and leftover spices adding points. (Plan B Games, 2024).

Wingspan.

EC: Birds improve habitat actions and add recurring powers. SP: Habitat rows determine activation; geometric adjacency is not scored. AS: Habitat activations chain powers after prerequisite food and egg investments. OC: Food supply, bird offers, and round-goal races are shared. HI: Bird hands and bonus cards create recurring private information. SC: Bird points, eggs, cached food, tucked cards, and goals interact. (Stonemaier Games, n.d.).

Azul.

EC: Wall tiles score but do not produce resources or stronger actions. SP: Pattern-line capacity and wall adjacency govern placement and points. AS: Pattern lines must fill before tiles transfer to the wall. OC: Drafts reshape compulsory leftovers and possible floor penalties. HI: Boards and draft pools are public; bag randomness is excluded. SC: Adjacency scoring, row/column/color bonuses, and penalties interact. (Next Move Games, n.d.).

Harmonies.

EC: Landscape and animal pieces score without increasing action productivity. SP: Hex adjacency and stack heights define habitats and terrain scores. AS: Required landscape patterns must precede animal placements. OC: Token groups and animal offers are shared. HI: Personal landscapes and selected animal cards are public. SC: Animal habitats overlap with several terrain-specific scoring patterns. (Libellud, n.d.).

Carcassonne.

EC: Features score and recycle followers but do not create a production engine. SP: Shared terrain connectivity determines legal placement and features. AS: Completions release followers; fields retain commitments until the end. OC: Merging features can create majority contests for ownership. HI: Placed tiles and followers are public; future tile draws are excluded. SC: Completed features, unfinished features, and field-city relationships differ. (Hans im Glück, n.d.).

7 Wonders.

EC: Production and commerce developments change future building access. SP: Neighbor identity matters, but there is no geometric placement puzzle. AS: Production, free-building chains, and age progression order investments. OC: Neighbor trade, military comparisons, and passed hands couple players. HI: Private draft hands and sealed selections are central. SC: Science sets, military comparisons, civic points, and commerce interact. (Repos Production, n.d.).

Castles of Burgundy.

EC: Mines and knowledge tiles add localized income or rule modifiers. SP: Estate adjacency, terrain, and connected regions constrain placements. AS: Acquisition, storage, placement, and immediate bonus actions form chains. OC: Shared depots and completion races couple otherwise personal estates. HI: Dice, tiles, and estates are public; future replenishment is excluded. SC: Region size, completion phase, animals, goods, and bonuses interact. (alea and Ravensburger, n.d.).

Brass: Birmingham.

EC: Industry investments raise recurring income and expand economic capacity. SP: Network connectivity governs resource access and expansion. AS: Financing, building, resource access, selling, and era changes form dependencies. OC: Players consume shared resources and use transport infrastructure. HI: Private location and industry cards constrain available builds. SC: Industry and link scoring are coordinated across canal and rail eras. (Roxley, n.d.).

Ark Nova.

EC: Sponsors, action upgrades, and zoo development improve later actions or income. SP: Enclosure packing and map constraints govern zoo construction. AS: Five action-card strength positions cycle as cards are used. OC: Shared displays, projects, and race timing dominate the selected profile. HI: Private animal/sponsor hands and final-scoring cards affect plans. SC: Appeal, conservation, project thresholds, and final scoring interact. (Feuerland Spiele, 2022).

Appendix C Comparison Scope and Horizon Reporting

C.1 Comparison-table scope and sources

Table 1 distinguishes game scope, evaluated interaction, decision demands, and evaluation focus. Decision demands summarize rules and tasks; they are not measured capability scores. DECE’s interaction entry includes the supplementary player counts in Table 9. Its cross-game and resource analyses use the common three-player cohort.

Sources for Table 1.

GameBench covers spatial strategy, social deduction, and deck building (Costarelli et al., 2024, Section 3.2; Appendices F–G). MindGames reports two- through six-player settings (Wang et al., 2026, Section 3.2); FinBoardBench evaluates four-player financial board games (Hu et al., 2026b, Sections 2–3). PTCG-Bench uses five decks within one two-player card game and includes harness and resource analyses (Hua et al., 2026, Section 4; Appendices B, E–F). From Code to Play evaluates generated state-evaluation functions in search agents across twelve TAG games (Eberhardinger et al., 2024, Section V-G; Table VIII). LudoBench evaluates questions about fixed states in five tabletop games (Peper et al., 2026). The table uses GameBench v2, MindGames v1, FinBoardBench v1, PTCG-Bench v2, From Code to Play v2, and the ICLR 2026 LudoBench release.

C.2 Observed decision lengths

Table 8 uses the same 480 three-player matches as the primary performance matrix, with 48 matches per game. It summarizes the recorded whole-match decision counter DD, engine turns, and D/3D/3 using linear-interpolation quantiles. Median DD ranges from 54 in 7 Wonders to 473 in Ark Nova; Splendor and Brass have medians of 81 and 393.5. These are observed counters for the evaluated systems and schedules.

The counters retain their game-specific source semantics. Splendor’s decision counts use player turns and omit extra noble-selection decisions. In 7 Wonders, 18 synchronous drafting rounds correspond to 54–55 recorded decisions across three players. Brass has 54 player turns but several accepted sub-decisions within a turn. In other games the recorded turn counter may itself advance at the sub-decision level; equality of turn and decision counts does not imply comparable strategic units. A larger count can therefore reflect interface granularity as well as sustained interaction.

Dividing DD by three gives the within-match average over seats before taking the median. Actual individual-player trajectory lengths require accepted-action logs and seat attribution. Controller decisions and model tool calls are separate execution measures (Appendix E.2). These counters document the evaluated interaction scope; they do not measure strategic depth on a common scale across games.

Appendix D Complete Results and Statistical Protocol

D.1 Ten-game three-player cohort

The primary native comparison contains 480 three-player matches across ten games and 1,440 participant appearances. Each of 12 configurations appears 12 times per game, four times at each seat. Table 9 reports this common exposure and the additional player-count coverage.

The original cohort contributes 144 three-player matches and the seven-game expansion contributes 336. Adding the 252 supplementary matches gives 732 native matches. The separate 72-match bridge and 48-match within-Qwen-family study are excluded from these totals. The separate Random, Heuristic, and ISMCTS reference cohorts are also excluded from these native-cohort totals.

PWS measures the fraction of opponents outranked, with half credit for ties; the ten-game mean weights games equally. Elo adjusts for the observed comparison graph, so its ordering need not equal unadjusted PWS ordering. Table 10 provides all ten per-game Elo fits from the primary cohort. Their intervals and PWS uncertainty are documented in Appendices D.3 and D.6.

Source reconciliation and database checks are described once in Appendix D.7. Performance and resource comparisons use the same 480-match primary cohort (Appendix E).

D.2 Placement measurement for the primary cohort

For participant ii with rank ri​tr_{it} in an ntn_{t}-player match tt, define

ui​t=1nt−1​∑j≠i[𝟙​(ri​t<rj​t)+12​𝟙​(ri​t=rj​t)].u_{it}=\frac{1}{n_{t}-1}\sum_{j\neq i}\left[\mathbb{1}(r_{it}<r_{jt})+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{1}(r_{it}=r_{jt})\right]. (2)

This pairwise placement score credits tied opponents by one half. For the primary cohort, nt=3n_{t}=3 throughout. With Ti​gT_{ig} denoting participant ii’s 12 appearances in game gg, report

Si​g=1|Ti​g|​∑t∈Ti​gui​t,Si=110​∑g∈𝒢Si​g.S_{ig}=\frac{1}{|T_{ig}|}\sum_{t\in T_{ig}}u_{it},\qquad S_{i}=\frac{1}{10}\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}S_{ig}. (3)

The ten games receive equal weight. Supplementary two-/four-player matches, non-LLM baselines, and matched harness studies are separate from this estimand.

Whole-match resampling within each game retains co-players and final rankings together, recomputes cell means and equal-game averages, and refits Elo separately. Pointwise percentile intervals condition on the evaluated games and schedules.

D.3 Primary-cohort uncertainty and ranking agreement

The primary cohort contains 480 unique three-player matches, 1,440 participant appearances, and 120 participant–game cells. Each cell has 12 appearances, with four at each seat. Every PWS cell is computed from final ranks, with half credit for ties. The resulting 12 configuration means sum to 600 percentage points within each game before rounding.

Sampling intervals.

We draw 5,000 whole-match bootstrap samples separately within each of the ten games, using seed 20260924. Players, opponents, and terminal outcomes remain together. Each draw recomputes all game-specific PWS values, equal-game means, and the between-group configuration contrasts in Table 4. Games and group membership remain fixed. One draw omitted a configuration in Burgundy and was redrawn. The intervals are pointwise 95% percentile intervals. Table 11 reports aggregate PWS.

For Elo, each sample refits the same centered, penalized Bradley–Terry objective used for the point estimate. Three-player pair weights are 1/21/2, the unnormalized loss uses penalty 0.02​∑iθi2/20.02\sum_{i}\theta_{i}^{2}/2, and Elo equals 1500+400​θi/log⁡(10)1500+400\theta_{i}/\log(10). Newton optimization converges this objective. All bootstrap comparison graphs remain connected. Independent fits reproduce all 24 aggregate Elo estimates to one decimal place. For the original three-game cohort, equal-game/equal-player-count PWS estimates agree to four decimal places.

Supplementary leave-one-game-out check.

For each target game gg, average each configuration’s PWS over the other nine games and compare that ranking with its PWS ranking in gg using Kendall τb\tau_{b}, which handles ties. Pair-order accuracy excludes pairs tied in the target game and gives half credit when the training scores tie. No held-out outcomes enter the nine-game ranking. This analysis describes how configuration rankings transfer across the ten games.

Mean LOEO τb\tau_{b} is 0.664 and equal-game pair-order accuracy is 83.9%. For each game’s reliability control, 2,000 disjoint random splits divide its 48 matches into two 24-match sets, conditioned on all configurations appearing in both sets. Each split preserves complete matches but does not force equal seat or opponent exposure within each half. Mean split-half τb\tau_{b} is 0.469 across games; Splendor is 0.176 and Ark Nova is 0.687. The 5th–95th percentile split ranges appear in Table 12. LOEO uses full-game samples; the reliability control uses half-game samples.

Additional whole-match perturbations yield a 2.5th–97.5th percentile range of 0.480–0.639 for mean LOEO τb\tau_{b}, below the plug-in estimate. Rank discreteness and the extra sampling noise make this a sensitivity distribution rather than a calibrated confidence interval. The descriptive LOEO estimates indicate common overall strength alongside game-specific deviations.

D.4 Strategic specialization: definitions and descriptive checks

RQ1 uses the ten-game three-player PWS matrix and the corresponding Elo ratings estimated from the same completed matches. Figure 4 uses those same game-specific ratings. Rank each game’s Elo over the same 12 configurations; assign average ranks for ties when comparing PWS and Elo orderings. Table 13 shows the configurations discussed in the text.

Group definitions and interpretation.

The public-information spatial group combines spatial planning = 2 and hidden information = 0 in Appendix B: Azul, Harmonies, Carcassonne, and Burgundy. Games with spatial planning = 2 additionally include Brass and Ark Nova; the remaining games are Splendor, Century, Wingspan, and 7 Wonders. Games with hidden information = 2 comprise Wingspan, 7 Wonders, Brass, and Ark Nova. Hidden-information annotations exclude uncertainty about future draws, so public holdings do not imply deterministic gameplay. Groups overlap and contain different combinations of other mechanisms. The Century/Brass/Ark Nova and Azul/Harmonies/Carcassonne triads describe GPT-5.6-Terra’s performance profile across these games.

Concentration of configuration advantages.

For configurations AA and BB of the same model, define δg=100​(PWS^A,g−PWS^B,g)\delta_{g}=100(\widehat{\mathrm{PWS}}_{A,g}-\widehat{\mathrm{PWS}}_{B,g}). Let GG be the four public-information spatial games and HH the other six: Splendor, Century, Wingspan, 7 Wonders, Brass, and Ark Nova. Average games equally within each group and report

Δ¯G=1|G|​∑g∈Gδg,Δ¯H=1|H|​∑g∈Hδg,Γ=Δ¯G−Δ¯H.\overline{\Delta}_{G}=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\delta_{g},\qquad\overline{\Delta}_{H}=\frac{1}{|H|}\sum_{g\in H}\delta_{g},\qquad\Gamma=\overline{\Delta}_{G}-\overline{\Delta}_{H}. (4)

Table 4 includes all three nominal models with two native configurations: Qwen3.8-Max (Qwen Code minus OpenCode), GPT-5.6-Sol (Codex minus OpenCode), and DSV4-Pro (DSH minus OpenCode). Γ\Gamma distinguishes a group’s configuration advantage from the average advantage elsewhere. A uniform shift in δg\delta_{g} across all ten games cancels in Γ\Gamma. The reference group combines several game designs, and each model pair compares its own two harnesses. These are descriptive comparisons of complete configurations under their native opponent samples.

Game-composition sensitivity.

Omit one game at a time from whichever group contains it and recompute Γ\Gamma over the remaining games, preserving their group assignments. Across all ten deletions, the ranges are 23.0–36.1 pp for Qwen3.8-Max, −19.7-19.7–−9.7-9.7 pp for GPT-5.6-Sol, and −5.6-5.6–+1.9+1.9 pp for DSV4-Pro. These are descriptive ranges over game subsets, not confidence intervals.

Table 14 retains the within-group diagnostics. Each public-information spatial game has a positive Qwen Code–OpenCode PWS contrast, so every one-game deletion preserves a positive mean. For games with hidden information = 2, the negative mean disappears when Ark Nova is removed, showing that this game’s result drives the group average.

Metric agreement and uncertainty.

Within-game Spearman agreement between Elo and PWS ranks ranges from 0.975 to 0.998 across games. The two rankings derive from the same outcomes; their agreement checks sensitivity to the choice of ranking metric.

Pointwise 95% intervals for Γ\Gamma use 5,000 whole-match bootstrap resamples within each game (Appendix D.3). Each draw retains all co-players, recomputes configuration differences, and averages games within the fixed groups. The public-spatial minus other-games contrast is 29.7 pp [11.9, 46.9] for Qwen3.8-Max, −14.4-14.4 pp [−32.6-32.6, 4.2] for GPT-5.6-Sol, and −1.7-1.7 pp [−21.8-21.8, 18.1] for DSV4-Pro. Sampling intervals describe variation across matches; game deletion measures sensitivity to the selected games.

D.5 Complementary native-system contrasts

The ten-game mean GPT-5.6-Sol Codex–OpenCode difference is −0.2-0.2 pp [−9.3-9.3, 8.6], despite game-level differences ranging from −20.8-20.8 in Century to +29.2+29.2 in Brass. Qwen3.8-Max / Qwen Code minus OpenCode averages +11.9+11.9 pp [3.2, 20.5], ranging from −33.3-33.3 in Ark Nova to +41.7+41.7 in Burgundy. DSV4-Pro / DSH minus OpenCode averages +6.3+6.3 pp [−3.6-3.6, 16.0]. These full-game profiles complement the group concentrations in Table 4.

D.6 Ten-game performance with uncertainty

Figure 7 and Table 15 expand the main performance matrix to show uncertainty for all 120 configuration–game cells in the 480-match three-player cohort. Each cell has 12 appearances; the ten-game mean and its interval appear in Table 11.

D.7 Cohort provenance and reproducibility

The native study includes 396 matches in the original cohort and 336 in the expansion. We reconcile individual match results with the combined outcome records and check each match’s game, player count, roster, seats, and seed against the schedule. All 732 final game records pass integrity checks and agree on match identity, game, rules version, seed, and terminal status. Their 528 stored terminal ranking events agree with the reported ranks; Splendor and Century rankings agree between individual and combined outcome records. Checksums verify all 672 result and game-state records in the expansion.

Deterministic analyses compute all 120 primary PWS cells from final ranks, fit per-game Elo, and generate 5,000 whole-match bootstrap replicates and the supplementary ranking diagnostics. Independent calculations reproduce aggregate PWS and Elo estimates to rounding precision. The native configuration contrasts use the same whole-match draws. All 120 per-game and 12 equal-game PWS intervals reconcile exactly.

DECE supports replay and resume through persisted game states and execution records. The analysis associates each scheduled match with its final terminal outcome. Native telemetry covers all 540 Codex appearances across the two source cohorts, including 360 in the primary three-player cohort. Native session records also cover six GPT-5.6-Sol / OpenCode appearances. The resource accounting and verification procedures are described in Appendix E.

Matched schedules and separate baseline records reproduce PWS for all 180 non-LLM reference matches (Appendix D.8). The native performance, horizon, execution, and same-model contrast figures use the ten-game three-player cohort. Additional player-count analyses remain separate; their coverage is explicitly limited to observed strata.

The within-Qwen-family study includes 48 complete outcomes and 24 matched harness pairs, with independent outcome verification (Appendix G.3). Its final game records pass integrity and terminal-identity checks, and all focal PWS values agree with exact rank-based arithmetic. Figure 3 and the within-Qwen-family statistics are computed directly from the matched outcomes.

D.8 Non-LLM reference baselines

Random samples uniformly from legal-action entries. Heuristic uses fixed, game-specific action scores with an ϵ\epsilon-greedy policy (ϵ=0.1\epsilon=0.1; Sutton and Barto, 2018, Section 2.2), without tree search. ISMCTS uses these scores for rollouts in single-observer information set Monte Carlo tree search (Cowling et al., 2012). It accesses the native simulator with at most 1,024 simulations and 18 search steps per decision, under a 30-second wall-time target.

The completed study contains 180 three-player matches: 60 per baseline and six per game, each against two LLM opponents. Opponents, seeds, rules, and focal seats match across the three baseline schedules. Each LLM configuration appears once per game; each baseline occupies every seat twice. These cohorts are separate from the main PWS, Elo, cross-game, and resource analyses.

The ten-game mean PWS is 0.8% for Random, 10.0% for Heuristic, and 44.6% for ISMCTS.

Appendix E Elo and Resource-Efficiency Protocol

E.1 Cohort-aligned recorded resource profiles

Figures 4 and 9 use the same 480 three-player matches as the primary performance table: 48 per game, 12 appearances per configuration/game, and 1,440 appearances overall. Resource records are joined to the audited outcome ledger by final match ID, seat, and participant identity. No two- or four-player cost is included, and non-LLM baselines and the matched-bridge cohort are excluded.

The estimand is recorded consumption associated with a final successful match ID, including retained native responses, recorded controller usage, and observable continuations. Replaced match IDs are outside this estimand.

E.2 Native execution demand and usage coverage

Figure 8 joins recorded controller decisions and normalized token use to all 1,440 participant appearances in the same 480 matches. Table 16 reports usage coverage from controller summaries and from the combined controller and native session records.

Controller decisions, engine decisions, and native model responses are separate units. A saved controller decision may contain several tool calls, and native usage can be available even when the controller summary lacks a token total. Usage accounting combines verified Codex native records, incremental controller usage where available, and Qwen Code native session totals or deduplicated native API responses. Input totals include cached input; output totals include reasoning when reported as a subset. All 1,440 appearances have quantified usage. The accounting scope, price scenario, and resource uncertainty are defined in Appendix E.

E.3 Accounting adapters and verification

Codex.

Original-cohort usage is computed from cumulative native session counters. Duplicate snapshots contribute zero; increments and resets are checked against last-response usage before summation. The expansion instead sums unique native responses and checks them against source-log entries and seat totals. Together these sources cover all 360 primary Codex appearances. Native responses and controller decisions remain distinct units.

Qwen Code.

We use native session totals for the 36 original three-player appearances and native API responses for the 84 expansion appearances. Expansion records are deduplicated by match, seat, session, and response ID, including context-compression requests. Incremental controller usage is not treated as a cumulative session total.

OpenCode and DSH.

We use incremental controller usage for the original three-game cohort. For the seven-game expansion, we reconcile all OpenCode and DSH appearances against native responses, including retained continuations and delegated calls. Copied session histories are counted once. Native session records for six GPT-5.6-Sol / OpenCode appearances agree with the recorded totals and are included once.

E.4 Frozen price scenario and token categories

Input includes cached input as a subset; output includes reasoning when reported as a subset. For an appearance with input II, cached input HH, and output OO, the recorded API-equivalent scenario cost is

C=10−6​{pin​(I−H)+pcache​H+pout​O}.C=10^{-6}\{p_{\rm in}(I-H)+p_{\rm cache}H+p_{\rm out}O\}. (5)

All categories are checked for nonnegativity and subset consistency. Input-plus-output token volume is I+OI+O: cached and reasoning tokens are not added again. Token volume is reported in each model’s native tokenizer.

The scenario uses DeepSeek busy-hour rates and the Qwen3.7-Plus promotional input tier. Context-length and cache-write surcharges and non-token charges are outside this scenario. Each configuration uses the same nominal-model API rates across harnesses. Rates are applied before aggregation, without rounding token means to millions.

E.5 Ratings, shared resampling, and descriptive frontiers

Elo uses the same Bradley–Terry fits as the performance analysis (Appendix D.3). Every unordered player pair contributes a comparison with half credit for ties. The weighted cross-entropy objective has penalty 0.02​∑iθi2/20.02\sum_{i}\theta_{i}^{2}/2 and ∑iθi=0\sum_{i}\theta_{i}=0; ratings are 1500+400​θi/log⁡(10)1500+400\theta_{i}/\log(10). Newton optimization converges this batch objective. Pair weights are 1/(n−1)=1/21/(n-1)=1/2 for the three-player figure; mixed-player-count fits use 1/[|𝒩g|​(n−1)]1/[|\mathcal{N}_{g}|(n-1)] to weight strata equally. There is no sequential KK-factor update.

The same 5,000 whole-match draws used for performance refit Elo and recompute mean cost and token volume within each game. Opponents, outcomes, and recorded costs stay together. Figure 9 averages game-level PWS and resource means equally, not separately centered Elo ratings. Whiskers are marginal pointwise 95% percentile intervals conditional on the tested games, recorded usage, and fixed prices.

A tested configuration is nondominated if no other has at least as high Elo and at most as much recorded cost, with one strict inequality. For mean-cost budget BB, the staircase in Figure 4 is

Vg(B)=maxi:Ci​g≤BEi​g,V_{g}(B)=\max_{i:\,C_{ig}\leq B}E_{ig}, (6)

where Ci​gC_{ig} is mean recorded cost and Ei​gE_{ig} is game-specific Elo. The envelope is defined where at least one configuration is affordable. Its steps select among tested configurations; BB constrains average cost, not the cost of every individual match. Elo/cost ratios are not used because Elo’s origin is arbitrary.

Frontier coverage and sampling stability.

For each configuration we count the games in whose point-estimate frontier it appears, then recompute nondominance in every joint whole-match resample. Table 20 reports these per-game resampling frequencies. Frontier coverage includes both low-cost and high-performance options. Frequencies describe sampling stability over the tested games and price schedule.

E.6 Performance–token frontiers

We repeat the frontier analysis using mean input-plus-output tokens per appearance in place of dollars. Cached input and reasoning remain subsets of input and output, respectively, and are counted once. The cohort, Elo estimates, and 5,000 joint whole-match draws are unchanged. This comparison removes price assumptions while retaining differences in tokenization, context reuse, and model computation. Native token counts do not represent equal compute across models.

Token frontiers contain one to six configurations per game. GPT-5.6-Sol/OpenCode appears in nine games under either resource measure. GPT-5.6-Luna/Codex appears on ten dollar frontiers and three token frontiers; DSV4-Pro/DSH appears on ten and two, respectively. The differences reflect the price and token mix as well as recorded volume. In 7 Wonders, GPT-5.6-Sol/OpenCode alone forms the token frontier: it has both the lowest mean token volume and the highest estimated Elo.

The cost and token analyses use identical outcomes, usage records, and bootstrap draws. Cost-frontier membership frequencies agree across the two implementations for all 120 configuration–game cells. An independent sorted-usage sweep verifies all 120 token membership decisions. Only the resource axis changes between the two analyses.

Appendix F Supplementary Player-Count Results

F.1 Full native-system panel

The supplementary cohort contains 252 matches in five additional game–player-count strata. Each configuration has 12 appearances per stratum, balanced across seats: six per seat at two players and three at four players. These results remain separate from the ten-game three-player performance and resource analyses.

Table 22 adds the observed two-/four-player strata to the ten-game three-player matrix in Table 3. In Splendor, Qwen3.8-Max / OpenCode leads the two-player PWS estimates (75.0%), whereas Qwen3.8-Max / Qwen Code leads at three and four players (70.8% and 80.6%). Across all 12 configurations, the two–three-player PWS-rank correlation is 0.070 in Splendor versus 0.701 in Brass; the three–four-player correlations are 0.792, 0.552, and 0.880 in Splendor, 7 Wonders, and Brass. Player-count mixtures can change the observed ordering within a game.

There is no uniform benefit from a larger table. DSV4-Pro / DSH’s Brass PWS rises from 29.2% to 75.0% between two and four players, while GPT-5.6-Sol / Codex moves from 100% to 91.7%. These are descriptive schedule-conditioned contrasts, since opponent composition also changes. These results motivate the fixed three-player main comparison.

Appendix G Matched Harness Studies

G.1 Design, evidence, and estimands

The bridge crosses DSV4-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash with two harnesses in two games, nine scenarios per game. Each scenario specifies one setup seed and one focal seat and contains four separate three-player matches. The other seats use DSV4-Flash / OpenCode and Qwen3.8-Flash / OpenCode as fixed opponents. The four focal configurations do not play one another in a single match. Comparisons therefore describe performance against this anchor population, not a four-participant league. The bridge uses the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 snapshot. Each focal seat occurs three times in every model–harness–game cell. The listed schedule places OpenCode first in 18 of the 36 harness pairs and Qwen Code first in 18.

The analysis includes 72 matches arranged into 36 matched harness pairs. We verify that each scheduled match has one result, with matching seeds, seats, and opponent configurations within each pair. We also check all paired score differences and aggregate point estimates. Every focal rank is 1, 2, or 3 and agrees with PWS Y=(3−rank)/2Y=(3-\mathrm{rank})/2 and the first-place indicator. These checks establish consistency between the schedule, focal outcomes, and summary statistics. Execution records and participant settings document the evaluated conditions (Appendix D.7).

For scenario bb in game gg, let Ym,h,g,bY_{m,h,g,b} be final focal PWS. The observed harness contrast and model-dependent contrast are

Δ^m,g\displaystyle\widehat{\Delta}_{m,g} =19​∑b=19(Ym,Qwen Code,g,b−Ym,OpenCode,g,b),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{9}\sum_{b=1}^{9}\left(Y_{m,\text{Qwen Code},g,b}-Y_{m,\text{OpenCode},g,b}\right), (7)
I^g\displaystyle\widehat{I}_{g} =Δ^Qwen3.8-Flash,g−Δ^DSV4-Flash,g.\displaystyle=\widehat{\Delta}_{\text{Qwen3.8-Flash},g}-\widehat{\Delta}_{\text{DSV4-Flash},g}. (8)

Overall contrasts average the two games equally. No raw game scores are pooled across titles. These estimands concern final competitive performance. Shared seeds do not imply shared subsequent trajectories: the focal changes can alter both opponents’ decisions and future states.

G.2 Uncertainty and observed ordering

We draw 100,000 bootstrap replicates with RNG seed 20260917. Within each game, nine scenarios are sampled with replacement, retaining all four model–harness outcomes from every selected scenario. This preserves the dependence needed for model comparisons and differences in harness gains. The two game means are averaged for pooled replicates. Intervals are pointwise empirical percentiles, conditional on the selected games and anchor configurations.

The point-estimate model ordering changes across harnesses, but the pooled model–harness contrast remains uncertain: I^=+30.6\widehat{I}=+30.6 pp, 95% interval [−5.6,69.4][-5.6,69.4]. Within Splendor it is +11.1+11.1 [−44.4,72.2][-44.4,72.2] pp; within 7 Wonders it is +50.0+50.0 [11.1,100.0][11.1,100.0] pp. The difference between these game-specific contrasts is +38.9+38.9 pp [−38.9,116.7][-38.9,116.7], not a resolved three-way interaction. As a sensitivity check for the family of four model–game harness contrasts, 98.75% percentile intervals are used at the nominal Bonferroni level. Qwen3.8-Flash’s 7 Wonders interval becomes [0.0,83.3][0.0,83.3] pp; all four include zero.

G.3 48-match within-Qwen-family study

Design and scope.

The independent study contains 48 complete three-player matches: Qwen3.8-Flash and Qwen3.8-Max, OpenCode and Qwen Code, Splendor and 7 Wonders, and six scenarios per game. Each scenario fixes the seed and focal seat across four configurations, using each seat twice per model–harness–game cell. Anchors are Qwen3.8-Flash / OpenCode and Qwen3.8-Max / OpenCode, with separate seat-scoped sessions. The frozen schedule randomizes scenario and configuration order. Matches start with independent workspaces and native sessions, a 1,200-second external-process limit per decision, and at most 32 concurrent matches. Registered model identifiers and effort settings are constant across harnesses.

Paired outcomes.

Let Ym,h,g,bY_{m,h,g,b} be the focal player’s PWS in a complete match. For this study, the harness contrast is Δ^m,g=16​∑b=16(Ym,Qwen Code,g,b−Ym,OpenCode,g,b)\widehat{\Delta}_{m,g}=\frac{1}{6}\sum_{b=1}^{6}(Y_{m,\text{Qwen Code},g,b}-Y_{m,\text{OpenCode},g,b}). The model contrast is I^g=Δ^Qwen3.8-Max,g−Δ^Qwen3.8-Flash,g\widehat{I}_{g}=\widehat{\Delta}_{\text{Qwen3.8-Max},g}-\widehat{\Delta}_{\text{Qwen3.8-Flash},g}. This direction differs from the cross-model-family contrast only in its model panel. Different anchors keep the studies separate despite their shared Qwen3.8-Flash identifier. Neither contributes to native Elo fits.

Uncertainty and multiplicity.

We enumerate all 66=46,6566^{6}=46{,}656 ordered bootstrap resamples within each game, retaining the four configurations together in every selected scenario. Figure 3b–d and Table 25 show the resulting paired estimates. All six Qwen3.8-Max/Splendor pairs improve, by 100 pp in one scenario and 50 pp in the other five. The two-sided sign-test value is p=0.03125p=0.03125 before adjustment and 0.1250.125 under a Bonferroni correction for the four model–game harness contrasts. The corresponding Qwen3.8-Max-minus-Qwen3.8-Flash gain is +50.0 pp [16.7, 83.3], but only four scenarios have nonzero interaction differences; their two-sided sign test gives p=0.125p=0.125. In 7 Wonders, the interaction is −8.3-8.3 pp [−83.3-83.3, 66.7].

Paired placements.

Qwen3.8-Max’s first/second/third counts in Splendor are 5/1/0 under Qwen Code versus 0/4/2 under OpenCode; in 7 Wonders it wins four of six under either harness. Qwen3.8-Flash’s paired changes are mixed in both games (Figure 3c).

Outcome verification.

The outcome ledger contains 48 matches and 24 harness pairs. Exact rational arithmetic reconciles every PWS with the terminal ranks. All 48 final game records pass integrity checks and match the stored identity, rules version, seed, terminal status, and turn count. Paired statistics, Table 25, and Figure 3 are computed directly from these outcomes. Checksums verify source-record integrity.
